relevant_group_routes.relationship: Orientalism as discourse and as a style of domination: Western knowledge and representation of 'the Orient' read through knowledge and power, extended to contrapuntal reading of the metropolitan canon with empire (1978–93)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. Orientalism (New York: Pantheon, 1978, first edition; page images checked): 'The Orient was almost a European invention' (p. 1); Orientalism as 'a style of thought based upon an ontological and epistemological distinction made between "the Orient" and (most of the time) "the Occident"' (p. 2) and as 'a Western style for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient' (p. 3). He qualifies it at once: 'it would be wrong to conclude that the Orient was essentially an idea, or a creation with no corresponding reality'; 'The relationship between Occident and Orient is a relationship of power, of domination, of varying degrees of a complex hegemony' (p. 5); and he leaves open 'how one can study other cultures and peoples from a libertarian, or a nonrepressive and nonmanipulative, perspective. But then one would have to rethink the whole complex problem of knowledge and power' (p. 24). Covering Islam (1981, introduction, p. ix): 'The underlying theme of Orientalism is the affiliation of knowledge with power.' 'Orientalism Reconsidered', Cultural Critique 1 (1985), read in full: the issues are 'the representation of other cultures, societies, histories; the relationship between power and knowledge' (p. 89); 'what for the most part got left out of Orientalism was precisely the very history that resisted its ideological as well as political encroachments' (p. 94); 'Orientalism is a praxis of the same sort, albeit in different territories, as male gender dominance, or patriarchy' (p. 103). Culture and Imperialism (New York: Knopf, 1993, first edition): 'What I left out of Orientalism was that response to Western dominance which culminated in the great movement of decolonization' (p. xii); 'we begin to reread it not univocally but contrapuntally, with a simultaneous awareness both of the metropolitan history that is narrated and of those other histories against which (and together with which) the dominating discourse acts' (p. 51); 'contrapuntal reading must take account of both processes, that of imperialism and that of resistance to it' (p. 66). In-period reception and criticism. Bernard Lewis, 'The Question of Orientalism', New York Review of Books, 24 June 1982 (web text, read in full, no page numbers): 'To prove this point, Mr. Said makes a number of very arbitrary decisions. His Orient is reduced to the Middle East, and his Middle East to a part of the Arab world'; 'a history of Arabic studies in Europe without the Germans makes as much sense as would a history of European music or philosophy with the same omission'; 'The most rigorous and penetrating critique of Orientalist scholarship has always been and will remain that of the Orientalists themselves.' Said's reply (NYRB, 12 August 1982): 'It is idiotic to say that Orientalism is a conspiracy or to suggest that "the West" is evil', while its 'modern discourse is correctly perceived as a discourse of power'; Lewis answered that 'It is difficult to argue with a scream of rage' and that the book 'takes a genuine problem of real importance, and reduces it to the level of political polemic and personal abuse'. Sadik Jalal al-'Azm, 'Orientalism and Orientalism in Reverse', Khamsin 8 (1981) (web text, read in full) credits 'laying bare Orientalism's persistent belief that there exists a radical ontological difference' between Orient and Occident, but holds that tracing Orientalism back to Homer 'simply lends strength to the essentialistic categories of "Orient" and "Occident"'. Rosalind O'Hanlon and David Washbrook (CSSH 1992; first-page extract only, as recorded in its source note) call Said's blend of themes 'virtually a paradigm for a new generation of historians and anthropologists' in Indian colonial history. Cheryl McEwan, Journal of Historical Geography 22 (1996), read in full: 'The inspiration behind the critical interest in empire, knowledge and power was undoubtedly Edward Said's groundbreaking and provocative Orientalism' (p. 489); feminist scholars 'argue that the critics of Orientalism and ethnocentric scholarship continue to write out gender' (p. 489); Reina Lewis's Gendering Orientalism (1996) is 'a response to Said in its efforts to destabilize the homogenizing tendencies of twentieth-century critiques of Orientalism' (p. 490). Said answered Dennis Porter's charge that he is 'ahistorical and inconsistent' as 'more weighty in assertion than it is in proof' (1985, p. 90); Porter's essay (1983) was not read. Not read: James Clifford's review essay (History and Theory 19, 1980) and Lata Mani and Ruth Frankenberg, 'The Challenge of Orientalism' (Economy and Society 14, 1985); both are recorded as metadata only. Later reading, labelled: Robert Irwin (2006, p. 299) writes that 'Early reviews of Orientalism were mostly hostile'. A contribution to postcolonial critique; the evidence does not make him its founder. edge_107 (language → post), edge_419 (post → indigenous) and edge_693 (post → geography) name him as a resource for others and stay.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: The agricultural-crisis thesis and its portrait of a routine-bound peasantry rejected by Paquet and Wallot (1972), criticised from Montreal by Tousignant (1980) and answered by Greer (1981; and in his 1993 book, as characterised by Dessureault, 1998, and Cardinal, 1999)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: This arrow represents Paquet and Wallot's, Tousignant's and Greer's specified interventions in the agricultural-crisis debate (quebec_historiography/agricultural_crisis_debate), not a verdict of the field, which includes Ouellet and his supporters. Paquet and Wallot (RHAF 1972, read in full): of the 1962 article, 'Cet article contient bien plus une intuition qu'une démonstration' (p. 193); Ouellet's postulates include 'le conservatisme invétéré des habitants, nous dirions même leur irrationalité' (p. 195); 'Comme la plupart de ses prédécesseurs, Ouellet peint les habitants comme des paysans essentiellement conservateurs, peu enclins à innover et désespérément embourbés dans des traditions routinières. Il s'agit là, nous semble-t-il, d'une simplification trop fréquente dans l'historiographie et qui appelle des réserves sérieuses' (pp. 201–202); 'Il n'existe pas de rationalité illimitée' (p. 202); 'les habitants ont adopté un régime agraire rationnel' (p. 221); their alternative, the Canadiens as 'd'astucieux politiques' in an 'équilibre conflictuel' with the British party (pp. 235–236), sought 'au-delà d'un économisme grossier' (p. 236); verdict, 'renvoyer comme irrecevable la thèse Ouellet' (p. 237), with the qualification that 'Quant à savoir si le débat est résolu pour autant, nous ne saurions le dire' (p. 237). Pierre Tousignant (RHAF 1980, read in full), on Le Bas-Canada (1976): the 1966 book 'faisait écho aux vieux préjugés de l'historiographie canadienne-anglaise tout imprégnée de l'idéologie de supériorité de la race anglo-saxonne', but the approach 'qui justifiait la notion désormais dépassée du «retard des mentalités» n'apparaît plus au premier plan dans Le Bas-Canada. C'est une notable amélioration' (p. 416); the periodisation of the export series 'n'est évidemment pas innocent' (p. 417); 'Il ne saurait plus être question de porter au seul compte d'une différence de mentalités l'appauvrissement progressif de la majeure partie de la paysannerie' (p. 419); 'Le professeur Ouellet nourrit de telles préventions contre le parti patriote qu'il a développé des réflexes défensifs à l'égard du parti bureaucrate' (p. 430); yet the book gives 'une intelligibilité vivante' to the period (p. 436, after Nicole Gagnon). Allan Greer (CHA Historical Papers 1981, read in full; n. 41 cites Ouellet's Lower Canada, 1980): 'The dominant explanation of Lower Canada's rural crisis emphasizes two factors, one demographic, the other cultural ... the atavistic mentality of the French-Canadian habitants led to their irrational refusal to accept technical improvements' (p. 213); 'The case of Sorel seems to challenge both elements of this interpretation'; 'To echo the commercial bourgeoisie of Lower Canada in blaming the habitants for their own agrarian predicament would be adding ideological insult to economic injury' (p. 214). On the rebellion, Greer's 1993 book is unread; reviewers say (their words): it 'brise nettement avec les travaux antérieurs de William H. Parker et de Fernand Ouellet pour qui la paysannerie était essentiellement victime de la crise économique et manipulée par des élites ultranationalistes' (Dessureault 1998, p. 206); 'à plusieurs reprises, A. Greer s'en prend aux arguments de cet historien, selon lesquels les habitants canadiens-français avaient une mentalité arriérée' (Cardinal 1999, p. 185). Ouellet's reply (1976, read): his critics 'ont réduit notre analyse à un simple rapport entre nationalisme et malaise agricole' and made the debate 'presque stérile' (p. 116); 'Le débat ne mérite plus d'être poursuivi; c'est la recherche qui exige de l'être' (p. 132). Le Goff's review of the controversy (CHR 1974) is unread; Ouellet reports that it concluded for a crisis from the early nineteenth century (1985, p. 25), so Le Goff is not counted among these critics.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Moral economies of science: certain forms of empiricism, quantification and objectivity “require” a web of affect-saturated values (1995)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own words, read (Osiris 10, 1995, pp. 3–4). "certain forms of empiricism, quantification, and objectivity itself are not simply compatible with moral economies; they require moral economies" (p. 3); a moral economy is "a web of affect-saturated values that stand and function in well-defined relationship to one another" (p. 4). n. 2 gathers studies by Hannaway, Porter, Schaffer and Shapin under the rubric. A distinct contribution from the 1992 image article (edge_761); the later book Objectivity (2007, with Galison) is dated in the chronology and read only through a reviewer.
